title.full: Canada’s Energy Future 2026: Energy Supply and Demand Projections to 2050

description: Exploratory case with lower GDP growth, LNG exports, data-centre load and prices.
pathwayDescription:
The Lower scenario is one of two scenarios new in EF2026 that bracket Current Measures to explore economic and energy uncertainty. Keeping the same climate policies and technology costs, it assumes lowter growth in four key drivers: real GDP growth (~1.2%/yr), one additional LNG project (4.25 Bcf/d), 1.5 GW of data-centre load by 2050 and lower global oil and gas prices (Brent ~US$55/bbl). End-use demand is about 10% below Current Measures and broadly flat versus 2023, oil output declines to about 5.2 MMb/d, gas reaches around 21–22 Bcf/d, electricity demand grows about 30%, and emissions end 9% below Current Measures (35% below 2005).

The CER is in charge of regulating construction and operation of energy assets and transport, export and trade of energy, exploration and siting activities. One if its responsibilities is to provide fact-based information on energy markets and supply as part of the Energy Information Program.

coreDrivers.policies: As in Current Measures, policies in place by Nov 2025 shape the baseline. Industrial carbon price rises to $170/t by 2030, then flat. Clean Electricity Regulations push non-emitting generation above 96% by 2050 with clean fuel, vehicle, efficiency, methane and HFC rules on top. Passenger ZEV represents 60% of sales by 2030, and 100% by 2035. Investment Tax Credits lower CCUS, hydrogen and clean power costs. With lower activity the same policies leave emissions 9% below Current Measures in 2050.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Electricity capacity is chosen by a least-cost model, so unit capital costs steer the build. Baseline cost views from NREL ATB 2024, EIA and IEA decline from 2024 to 2050: onshore wind by 23%, solar by 38%, NG with CCUS by 24%, and SMR  by 37%; with only ~30% demand growth the least-cost build adds ~55 GW onshore wind, 3.0 GW SMR and 5.75 GW NG with CCUS by 2050, the smallest additions of any scenario, with wind at 23% of generation.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Differentiating driver to Current Measure: weaker export demand cuts ~0.4 pp/yr from GDP growth versus Current Measures (1.2%/yr; population 0.5%/yr to 47 M; CPI 2.0%). GDP is ~10% (> $450 bn) below Current Measures in 2050, so end-use demand is ~10% lower and broadly flat versus 2023.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Lower market drivers: Brent ~US$55/bbl from 2030, Henry Hub dipping to ~$2.75 by 2030. 1 LNG project and 1.5GW of data center loads are needed by 2050.

dependencies.dependency_description: The same Clean Electricity Regulations and ITCs apply, but with only ~30% demand growth less new clean capacity is needed; the grid still exceeds 96% non-emitting and power emissions fall 73% vs 2025. Policy shapes the electricity mix more than the pace of expansion.

Regulatory exposure as in Current Measures (Clean Electricity Regulations flexibility, possible Alberta MOU changes, rate-based cost recovery) but with the smallest build and gas fleet (32.7 GW unabated), so rule changes would shift outcomes least.
Spending averages  around $30 bn/year, below the 2006–2023 average of $32 bn/yr and dipping to $24 bn/yr in 2036–45; the financing burden on ratepayers is the lightest of any scenario.
The report does not model opposition. Indigenous engagement found communities favour renewables and some SMRs but want cultural sites preserved.

As in Current Measures, behaviour is exogenous: lower load growth (~30%, near the historical 1%/yr) comes from slower GDP and light data-centre growth. No consumer-behaviour constraint is described beyond the general exclusion of demand-side management.

The same ~70% Interprovincial transfer  expansion applies, but with 23% wind share in the generation technology mix and 15.8 GW of batteries the flexibility requirement is the lowest of the scenarios. As in other scenario, Canada–US interconnection capacity is held constant.

Emerging technologies play a smaller role: 3.0 GW SMR (half of Current Measure build-out), 5.75 GW gas-CCUS (75% of Current Measure build out), 1.8 GW hydrogen-fired (half of Current Measure build-out), 15.8 GW batteries by 2050 (2/3 of Current Measure build-out), with mature hydro and wind doing most of the work. Lower demand mostly diminish pathway dependecy to hydroigen market-readiness.

Clean-power components depend on concentrated global supply chains (China provide more than 80% of solar modules, 70–80% of wind blades; graphite and lithium processing). The report doesn't provide any quantitative data for raw input needs for the Lower Scenario.

No hourly infrastructure is modelled for this variant, but with lower wind deployment, the system is less dependent on wind availability, and gas would fill demand during no-wind period. Hydro output would also vary with precipitation but the models do not otherwise include climate-change impacts.

Accelerating electricity installations could face skilled-labour shortages. Electricity Human Resources Canada projects 17,000–28,000 sector job openings in 2023–2028 against 110,600 jobs, and acute shortages could delay new generation and raise costs.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Electricity economic-sector GHG, Mt CO2e, national only (no provincial split). Residual unabated gas runs under Clean Electricity Regulations compliance flexibility (p.51).

Installed capacity MW, Canada and provinces. Storage is battery only (‘Battery Storage’); pumped hydro is not separated and appears to sit within Hydro. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis. Includes wind dedicated to hydrogen production.

Derived: electricity-sector Mt CO2e (national inventory basis, direct, CO2e) ÷ total generation incl. distributed solar and wind dedicated to hydrogen; captive industrial generation not separately identified, so numerator and denominator may not align.
Generation GWh, Canada and provinces; includes distributed solar and wind dedicated to electrolysis. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis.
Capital and repair expenditure, C$2025, bulk power system only; excludes distribution and transmission other than generation connections and interties (p.88).
Overnight capital costs for onshore wind, utility solar, NG with CCUS and SMR; no storage, hydro or O&M costs disclosed; no cost file in the Open Government dataset.
Derived share of generation by technology (each technology ÷ ‘Total’); boundary as Generation.

Transfer capacity only stated in prose (~70% more interprovincial capacity by 2050 in all scenarios). Annual flows (not lines) are in electricity-interchange-2026.csv. Canada–US capacity fixed; distribution excluded.
